parsed.study_design: Comparative case study of two urban development project implementations
parsed.population_and_sample: Approximately 2,600 resettled families in Mirpur, Dhaka, and 45,200 residents served by 20 water projects in marginal neighborhoods of Tegucigalpa by 1990
parsed.exposure: Project governance and implementation arrangements, including agency coordination, creation of the UEBM, community water boards and participation, financing and cost-recovery rules, technology choices, and political intervention
parsed.outcome: Completion and continued operation of water and sanitation infrastructure; household or community access through yard or public taps; water affordability; system maintenance; and project financial viability
parsed.rationale: The paper presents two identifiable project case studies and evaluates implementation using documentary and reported project evidence. In the Tegucigalpa case, pp. 33–36 report baseline exclusion and high vendor prices, describe the UEBM and community-governance arrangements, and state that 20 projects served 45,200 people through yard or public taps and were financially viable. The Mirpur case reports provision of tubewells, hand pumps, and latrines to about 2,600 families, while documenting institutional delays and post-completion maintenance failures on pp. 32–33.
